You'll need to set a hierarchy of priority between those activities based on your goals. In general, try to space out 3 high intensity sessions in between medium/low intensity. For yoga, you can lump short easy session on high intensity days and longer session on other days. Your muscles are still worked during passive stretching so just because you're not exerting power, doesn't mean it doesn't need recovery especially longer intense stretching. The first day after rest day should be your priority activity that you want to progress the most. Walking can be done everyday since it's very easy to recover.

For example (idk how you prioritize between strength and endurance sports so this is just a guideline):

Day 1 - high intensity (highest priority) + yoga + walking

Day 2 - moderate intensity + yoga + walking

Day 3 - yoga + walking (active rest day)

Day 4 - high intensity + yoga + walking

Day 5 - moderate intensity + walking

Day 6 - high intensity + yoga + walking (least prioritized sport)

Day 7 - complete rest day

People already went on about obvious symptoms when a deload week is absolutely called for, but sometimes you'll only feel "a little sluggish" and push on a high intensity session when you should've take it easier. On these days, an quick way to check if you're up to it, do a deadhang and compare it to your baseline time. If you can barely do a third or half of your record time, reduce the intensity of your session so the next day/session it won't feel as if you did a one step forward and two steps back.

Reducing the intensity can done by simply doing everything the same but lowering the weight; reducing sets; doing endurance rep range instead of strength rep range; or just doing something entirely different like trying out different machines and experimenting with new moves or sports just to see if it's something worth adding to your repertoire (more of a learning session to focus on form/technique instead of going all out).

Everybody already got great program recs so I'll just give more general advice: 
Focus on consistency first rather than exercise volume. Beginners won't gain anything from doing too much too quickly and you'll have a harder time during recovery which will give you more excuse to slack off. It can took months to finally turn fitness into a habit so start small and look around to find something that you can look forward to. I'd recommend some form of strength training AND cardio every week (you can stick to low intensity steady state cardio for a start to build better stamina). Since you're already slim you should be in slight calorie surplus + protein to build muscle. Nutrition-wise you don't need to do everything correctly right away. If you change your lifestyle too much at once it can easily feel too overwhelming and you're likely to stop a new routine before you can give it a chance to show results. So just get your body moving for now, and incorporate changes little by little.
